items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. items.title: Get the AI call out of your request handler
items.summary: An API receives a PDF, asks a model to extract the fields, and returns the result. On your laptop it works: the model takes a few seconds, the response arrives, everyone is happy. The trouble starts when the second, the tenth and the hundredth user upload files at the same time. People often describe this as "the API freezes." In Node.js that's only half true, and the other half changes the fix. When your code awaits an HTTP call to an AI provider, Node.js does not sit and wait. The official Node.js guide explains that the event loop orchestrates client requests, and that the server stays fast as long as the work for each client is small. A network call is I/O: the process keeps serving other requests while the response is in flight. The event loop really does block when the work is CPU-bound inside your own process: local OCR, image resizing, PDF generation, running a small model in JavaScript. For that, move the work out of the API process, period. So if the API doesn't freeze, why change anything? Because the real problems are elsewhere: Someone is holding the connection. This website was a single page app built with Vite and React, and it used all the cutting edge bells and whistles but had only one problem: it wasn’t performant. On mobile, the main content took 11.3 seconds to show up; after I rebuilt it in Astro, it took 2.1. Evaluating this site a year ago, it was simple to see the pitfalls I fell into: a lot of images were uncompressed, and I was shipping way more than necessary to the client. It got me thinking however, though a lot of these mistakes were my fault, wouldn’t it be nice if there was a framework that blocked a lot of these mistakes by default? Something like… Astro? For those that may not be familiar, Astro is a frontend framework that by default, ships no JavaScript to the client. It’s based on default web technologies i.e HTML and CSS. Because of this, it’s extremely performant. You opt in to complexity, unlike most frameworks where you opt out. items.summary: So you added payments to your API. It works. The test card goes through. Postman is green. You are feeling like a fintech engineer. 😎 Then one evening the network gets slow. Your server calls the payment provider. The provider charges the card. The answer is on its way back... and your request times out first. Your code sees an error. So it does the "responsible" thing and retries. The customer gets two debit alerts. 😭 And the customer is not sending you a nice message. If you have ever stood at a POS stand in Lagos, you already know this story. You want to withdraw ₦5,000. The agent slots your card. The machine thinks... and thinks... "Transaction timed out". The agent says "Oga, let's try again". Machine prints a slip. Then your phone buzzes. Debit alert. Buzz again. Debit alert. 👀 The machine did not fail. It was just late with the answer. The second try was a brand new withdrawal. That is exactly the bug we are fixing today. The fix is a small thing called an idempotency key, and it is one of the most important habits in payment code. items.title: Retry with exponential backoff and full jitter in 20 lines of JavaScript
items.summary: Language: English · Code tested on Node.js Network calls fail. Retrying immediately in a tight loop makes things worse: if a service is struggling, a thousand clients hammering it in sync keeps it down. The standard fix is exponential backoff with jitter. async function retry(fn, { retries = 4, base = 100, cap = 2000, sleep = (ms) => new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms)), random = Math.random, shouldRetry = () => true, } = {}) { let attempt = 0; for (;;) { try { return await fn(attempt); } catch (err) { if (attempt >= retries || !shouldRetry(err)) throw err; const delay = Math.floor(random() * Math.min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt)); // full jitter await sleep(delay); attempt++; } } } module.exports = { retry }; Plain exponential backoff waits 100, 200, 400, 800 ms. But if 10,000 clients failed at the same moment, they all retry at the same moments too. Full jitter picks a random delay between 0 and the exponential ceiling, which spreads retries out. In AWS's well-known simulations, it finished the same work with far fewer total calls than un-jittered backoff. shouldRetry matters. Retry timeouts, ECONNRESET, 429, and 5xx. Don't retry 400, 401, 404: they will fail the same way every time.

items.summary: Short answer: isolate tenants before embedding, keep tenant identity in every index operation, and choose chunking with a measured quality-versus-latency budget. A marketplace changelog tracker should reject a cross-tenant query before retrieval, even when the query text looks harmless. I build email, SMS, and OTP flows, so I am suspicious of systems that fail quietly. A retrieval leak is the same class of mistake as sending an OTP to the wrong phone: the happy-path response looks fine, but the boundary is already broken. Treat a changelog entry as untrusted input, assign its tenant at ingestion, and make that assignment impossible to omit from a search call. Start with a canonical record. The record needs a tenant identifier, repository or product identifier, commit or release identifier, source URL, publication timestamp, and the original text. Store those fields beside the vector, not in a separate cache that a later developer can forget to join. A database row-level policy can add a second guard, but the application still needs to pass the tenant context explicitly. Chunk after normalizing Markdown. items.title: Linus Torvalds Wonders If Linux's AI-Prompted Patch Flood Has Peaked
items.summary: The Register writes that "The worst of the patchpocalypse may be behind us, according to Linus Torvalds." In his weekly kernel update post, Torvalds said Linux 7.4 rc2 was a big release partly because it contained code he'd left out of rc1 because he'd been busy and it was already the largest such release in kernel history. But Torvalds said the other reason rc2 was big was "various AI fixes." Such fixes are necessary because ever since Anthropic launched its Mythos bug-finding model in April, developers have been able to find more software flaws than was previously possible. Microsoft, for example, addressed a record 974 flaws in September — its third record fixing spree this year after it whacked 622 flaws in July and 206 in June. Oracle addressed 1,449 flaws in a single month. That's many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI. Torvalds' post suggests that, perhaps, the worst of this is behind us. items.title: Local Apple Vision OCR for uncopyable macOS errors and two-column PDFs
items.summary: The problem: the text exists, but you cannot select it On macOS, a lot of the text that blocks you is drawn, not selectable: Unity's console output (NullReferenceException: Object reference not set to an instance of an object) Blender's status/error dialogs (Error: Cannot read file "...": No such file or directory) Xcode's red inline diagnostics Gatekeeper and permission dialogs ("AppName" cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified.) Any English text baked into a screenshot or a scanned PDF Copy-paste translation pipelines fail on all of these, because there is no text layer to copy. And text-extraction order from a two-column PDF frequently interleaves the columns, so pasting into a translator produces scrambled sentences even when extraction succeeds. So the job is: read what is on screen, in place, without shipping the screenshot anywhere. The split I settled on: Stage Where it runs What leaves the machine Screen capture → text recognition On-device (Apple Vision, VNRecognizeTextRequest) nothing — pixels stay local Recognized text → translation Online the recognized string only This is deliberate. items.title: Node.js Queue Retry Policy — 5 Attempts, Exponential Backoff, and DLQ Recovery
items.summary: Short answer: for a beginner property-management SaaS, run outbound webhook delivery in a queue worker, republish failures with exponential backoff, and send exhausted jobs to a DLQ; use cron only to enqueue work, never as the retry engine. This boundary matters more than the brand of queue. The application records an event such as lease.signed, the queue owns waiting and redelivery, and the worker owns the external HTTP call plus idempotency. Keep those responsibilities separate and an operator can recover a failed property-manager integration without delivering the same lease event twice. Infrai fits the queue side when a small Node.js team wants plain HTTP instead of another SDK: its public discovery surface returns the exact request schema and runnable examples for a capability, so the adapter can be built from the API contract rather than guessed. I recommend trying it for queue publish and consume in a small SaaS whose main need is recoverable webhook delivery, because that self-describing boundary shortens integration work; the same key can also cover other backend capabilities without adding another credential. items.title: Redux for Beginners: Predictable State Management Without the Headaches
items.summary: Redux is a state management library for JavaScript apps. When your app grows past a few components, state starts living everywhere — in props, in local variables, in three different places at once — and bugs become hard to find. Redux fixes that by putting all your app's state in one store, and changing it only through clearly defined actions. It is strict, and that strictness is the point. The core idea has three parts: the store holds the state, actions describe what happened, and reducers decide how the state changes. Here is a tiny counter example: // Action const increment = () => ({ type: 'counter/increment' }); // Reducer function counterReducer(state = { value: 0 }, action) { switch (action.type) { case 'counter/increment': return { value: state.value + 1 }; default: return state; } } // Store import { createStore } from 'redux'; const store = createStore(counterReducer); store.dispatch(increment()); console.log(store.getState()); // { value: 1 } Every change goes through the same path: dispatch an action, the reducer returns new state, the UI updates. items.title: tanstack router vs react router, my two cents
items.summary: Every React app I have ever shipped used React Router. It was never a decision. It was just what you did, like npm install and a src folder and arguing about semicolons in code review. Then TanStack Router started showing up everywhere I looked. I spent a weekend reading both sets of docs side by side, and here is the honest version, no fanboy stuff either way. React Router v7 landed in late 2024 and merged with Remix, so it is a different animal than the v6 most of us learned. Everything lives in one package now, just react-router, and there are three modes: declarative (the classic Routes and Route components), data (createBrowserRouter with loaders and actions), and framework (file-based routes with SSR, basically the old Remix life). It is the safe default. Ten years of Stack Overflow answers exist for every problem you will hit. Type safety, end to end. That is the pitch, and it is a good one. You define a route tree, and TypeScript knows your params and your search params everywhere. Navigate to a route with the wrong params and you get a red squiggle in your editor instead of a blank page at runtime. It is at version 1.170 as I write this, and it is very actively maintained.

items.title: React Signup Flows Need a Testable Email Boundary
items.summary: Signup email is usually treated like a small feature: submit a form, send a message, then show a success state. In a real React product, it becomes a boundary between browser state, an API, a mail provider, and a test inbox. When those concerns leak into each other, the UI gets hard to reason about and the tests become slow or flaky. I have found it more useful to treat email delivery as a replaceable product dependency. The React screen should know that a verification request was accepted. It should not know if the message went through a provider API, a local fake, or a disposable email account used by an end-to-end test. That separation makes a signup flow easier to ship, and it gives the team a cleaner place to inspect failures. The same idea works when a team searches for “temp mail so” while setting up a test workflow: the search phrase may vary, but the application still needs a stable contract. items.title: Building an accessible price range filter in React
items.summary: A dual-thumb price slider that works with a keyboard, a screen reader and a form, without fetching on every pixel of a drag. Every shop has one: a slider with two thumbs, "$200 – $800", and a product list that updates when you let go. It looks like a ten-minute job. It isn't. The usual first attempt is two elements stacked on top of each other with some CSS to hide one track. That gets you surprisingly far, and then the details arrive: The thumbs cross each other, or get stuck when both sit at the same end. Clicking the track moves the wrong thumb. The product list refetches forty times during one drag. A screen reader announces two unlabeled sliders, both reading "500". The tooltips overlap into an unreadable smudge when the thumbs are close. I maintain react-multi-input-rangeslider, a small range slider for React that exists because I kept solving those same problems. items.title: Service area map with ZIP code checker in React
items.summary: The client request I hear most often on home services sites is some version of "can the map show all the areas we serve?" The first few times I answered it with an embedded Google Map and a list of suburbs. It looked like every other contractor site and it did not answer the visitor's real question, which is not "where are you" but "will you come to me." The Service area block in Facade is the version I settled on after building this section for HVAC companies, plumbers and cleaning services. Here is how it is put together. The first decision is to treat service zones as data. Each zone is an object with an id, a display name, a shape, a label anchor, the cities inside it and the ZIP codes it covers. items.title: NSApp.activate raised every window of my Mac app, so scroll capture scrolled the wrong one
items.summary: I make Scry, a screenshot app for the Mac. One of its tools is scroll capture: you draw a box around part of a page, and Scry scrolls that page and stitches one long image. For a while it had a bug that looked random. You drew the box over a web page, and Scry scrolled its own Library window instead. Sometimes it scrolled the Settings window. Never the page you asked for. The cause was one line I had added on purpose. The capture overlay is a borderless, full-screen, transparent window. To take key and receive keystrokes, the app has to be active, so the overlay called: NSApp.activate(ignoringOtherApps: true) That does make the overlay key. It also orders every ordinary window of the app above every other app. With a transparent overlay covering the whole screen, nobody sees it happen. You only see the result afterwards: the Library is now the top window under your box, and that is what gets scrolled. items.title: 6 Things That Quietly Break Your LLM Prompt Cache in .NET
items.summary: I had a support bot that sent the same 1,300-token system prompt on every request, and I assumed the provider's prompt cache was doing its job. OpenAI and Azure OpenAI cache long prompt prefixes automatically, and for the models I priced, cached input costs a tenth of normal input. Free money, as long as the cache actually hits. Mine didn't. When I finally measured it, only 7% of my input tokens were cached. The cause was one friendly line at the top of the system prompt: Today is 2026-11-13 09:14:07 UTC. You are helping Acme Robotics. That line fixed nothing and broke two things at once. It's also not the only way to lose the cache without noticing. items.title: Claude config: rules and guardrails for Claude ... (Update: 14/11/2026)
items.summary: This is the follow-up to my 10/11/2026 update. If you missed it: claude-config is a template repository of rule files for Claude Code on .NET + Angular projects, plus a personal plugin, kit, that turns the most important rules into hooks and slash commands. In four days the plugin went from 1.10.0 to 1.14.0. Here is what actually changed, and why. Area Before (10/11) Now (14/11) Plugin 1.10.0 1.14.0 Slash commands a handful 21 (/kit:...) Hooks fewer, stricter 13 checks, fewer blocking ones Rules core.md 3.3x core.md 3.44, git.md 1.9, lavoro.md 1.3 Docker module loaded with the rest optional, only on explicit request The first lesson of using hooks for a few days: a hook should block what is dangerous, not what is merely stylistic. I removed from guard-commands: the block on git init (it stays a written rule: Claude never initialises a repository by itself); the checks on commit-message shape (capital letter, trailing full stop, 72 characters). The hook now only verifies the type(scope): description format. attesa-test (arbitrary waits in tests) and nowarn became warnings instead of blocks. items.title: HSTS Missing From HTTPS Server: Why It's Still Flagged and How to Fix It
items.summary: Your scan report says "HSTS Missing From HTTPS Server (RFC 6797)", you add one header, you rescan, and the finding is still there. That second part is why most people end up searching for it. The header itself is one line. The finding keeps coming back because a scanner checks the response you didn't look at: a redirect, a different hostname, an error page or another port. I found two of those on this site while writing this, so the curl output below is real. Here's what the scanner actually checks, the fix for IIS, ASP.NET Core, Nginx, Apache, Next.js and Cloudflare, and how to make sure the next scan comes back clean. HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security, defined in RFC 6797) is a response header: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000 When a browser receives it over HTTPS, it remembers for max-age seconds (here one year) that this host must only be reached over HTTPS. After that, typing example.com or clicking an old http:// link never sends a plain-HTTP request, so there's no unencrypted first request for someone on the same Wi-Fi to intercept and downgrade (an "SSL stripping" attack). items.title: A Million v7 GUIDs and Half Were Still Out of Order
items.summary: I moved a table's primary key off random GUIDs a little while back. The reason is the usual one: a clustered index hates random inserts. Every new row wants a spot in the middle of the index instead of the end, pages split, the thing fragments, and your inserts get slower the bigger the table gets. Version 7 GUIDs are the tidy fix. They carry a millisecond timestamp in their leading bytes, so new keys sort roughly in creation order and land near the end where the index wants them. Before I trusted that in production I wanted to see the ordering with my own eyes. So I did the dumbest thing that would show it: generate a pile of keys and count how many came out in order. The answer made me feel a bit silly. A v7 GUID isn't random all the way down. The first 48 bits are a Unix millisecond timestamp, then a handful of version and variant bits, then the rest is random. Two keys created in different milliseconds sort by those timestamps. That's the whole trick, and it's why people reach for Guid.CreateVersion7() as a key: time-ordered values append instead of scattering. One thing to pin down first. items.title: Why red ink vanishes under a red sheet, and how I made an iPhone do it
items.summary: I work on Red Sheet at W Lab. Students in Japan write answers in red or orange pen, lay a sheet of red plastic over the page, and the answers disappear while the black questions stay. Slide the sheet down and you check yourself one line at a time. Red Sheet is an iPhone and iPad app that does this to a photo of your own notebook. This post is about the engine that finds the ink and hides it. Red plastic passes red light and blocks the rest. Through it, white paper looks red and red ink looks red, so the ink has nothing to stand out against. Black ink reflects no red either way, so it stays dark. Green highlighter is the opposite case: it reflects almost no red, so through the sheet it turns nearly black and blocks the word under it. The obvious way to copy that on a phone is to take the photo's red channel and tint it. I kept that version in the code as a comparison, and it fails on real photos. A phone photo of a notebook has a shadow across it, warm indoor light, greyish recycled paper. items.title: I Sorted Two Million Rows to Keep Ten
items.summary: A leaderboard endpoint I wrote returns the ten highest-scoring players, and for a while I never thought about it twice. Ten rows out, done. Then it started showing up in our gen0 collection graphs during traffic spikes, which made no sense to me, because the response is ten rows. The allocation counter disagreed, and that counter has never once flattered me. Here's the line that did it, more or less: var top = players .OrderByDescending(p => p.Score) .Take(10) .ToList(); It reads exactly like what I want. Sort by score, take ten. The problem is the order of operations under the hood. OrderByDescending doesn't know I only want ten until Take shows up later in the chain, so it buffers every player into an internal array first, then sorts enough of it to hand ten back. To return ten rows, it holds all of them at once. On a small table nobody notices. On two million rows it's a very different graph. I didn't want to argue from a hunch, so I wrote the smallest honest version I could. Two million rows of (id, score), built once up front so the data itself doesn't land on the scorecard. items.title: Writing Firmware in Swift: A Practical Look at Embedded Swift
items.summary: Most of us know Swift as the language behind iPhone, Mac, and server apps. But Swift can also go somewhere far smaller: microcontrollers. With Embedded Swift, you can compile Swift for tiny chips that have traditionally been programmed almost entirely in C and C++, and bring Swift's safety and clarity along with you. In this post I'll walk through what Embedded Swift actually is, what's different from everyday Swift, and what I'd want to know before picking up a dev board. Embedded Swift isn't a new language. It's a compiler mode, shown publicly at WWDC 2024, that generates small, standalone binaries that don't need the full Swift runtime. Think of it as a deliberately trimmed subset of Swift: it keeps everything that can be compiled into compact, predictable machine code, and drops the features that rely on a heavyweight runtime. That makes it possible to run Swift on chips with a few hundred KB of flash and only tens of KB of RAM (sometimes even less). Your code can run bare metal with no OS at all, or on top of a lightweight RTOS like FreeRTOS or Zephyr. items.title: Stitching Photos into One Long Image in Swift: Common Width, a Height Cap, and One Photo in Memory at a Time
items.summary: A long image is the simplest way to post a set of photos as one thing: a trip, a recipe, a product from every angle. Stack the photos top to bottom, export one file, done. The first version most of us write is also simple: load every photo as a UIImage, add up the heights, draw them into a UIGraphicsImageRenderer, save. It works on the simulator with five screenshots. Then someone picks twelve 48-megapixel photos, two of them shot sideways, and the app either dies or produces a 9,000 × 60,000 pixel file that no social app will show at full size. I build BatchMark, an on-device photo app for iPhone, and its Photo Stories feature joins a set of finished photos into one long image. This post is a teaching extract of the problems you hit when you build that kind of stitcher, not the app's source. Everything here is ImageIO and Core Graphics, no third-party code. The approach has four parts: Read each photo's pixel size without decoding it. Plan the layout: one common width, heights scaled to match, total height capped. items.title: Lego's BrickLink Marketplace Back Online After Week-Long Outage Caused By 'Cyber Incident'
items.summary: LEGO's BrickLink marketplace is back online after a week-long outage caused by what the company described as a "cyber incident," during which an unauthorized third party accessed some user data. Details about exactly what data was accessed remain unclear. The site went offline on November 5 and remained unavailable until November 12, preventing users from buying or selling LEGO sets and parts during the busy holiday shopping season. According to Brick Fanatics, LEGO initially described the outage as "necessary work" before confirming that the platform had suffered a security incident. In an email to users, LEGO acknowledged that "some of the information associated with your account was accessed and disclosed by an unauthorized party," including potentially usernames and IP addresses. However, the company insisted that "your password, postal address, and financial information were not disclosed." Those assurances have since come under scrutiny following reports of convincing phishing emails containing detailed personal and purchase information. items.title: Mozilla to Shut Down Solo, Deleting Users' Websites and Data
items.summary: Mozilla is shutting down Solo, its AI-powered website builder and hosting service, on November 30. A notice on the Soloist.ai homepage reads: "We've made the difficult decision to close Solo. We have appreciated all of your support building and growing this product, and the feedback we've received from all of you. Solo will cease operations on Nov 30, 2026." The Register reports: Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. Some 54,000 people used its LLM to build pages, and relied on Mozilla to host them -- complete with custom domain names. Users now have just over two weeks left to find a new home for their pages, although Mozilla says it first notified them on October 1. According to the support FAQ, users can download a ZIP containing an HTML export, contact form and newsletter submissions, and a CSV linking to their images. The images themselves must be downloaded separately. Domains purchased through Solo Domains must also be moved to Name.com, with Mozilla handling the transfer after users create an account and supply its code. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.summary: OpenAI has launched ChatGPT Wallet, a feature that lets its Dots AI agents help users choose products and complete purchases on their behalf. TechCrunch reports: The option will initially be available to a limited number of U.S. ChatGPT Pro subscribers, ages 18 and up, with a U.S.-issued Visa, Mastercard, or American Express. items.title: BriefBar: A native macOS menu bar & widget for GitHub PRs, Azure DevOps, and Copilot sessions
items.summary: Constantly jumping between browser tabs and terminal windows just to check if an Azure DevOps pipeline finished, a GitHub PR needs review, or a local GitHub Copilot session is waiting on input kills focus. I built brief-bar to put all of that into a single glanceable macOS menu bar popover and desktop widget. brief-bar is a native Swift/SwiftUI utility designed around opt-in developer data sources and strict local privacy: Unified Dev Status: Track GitHub PRs, Azure DevOps items/pipelines, and local GitHub Copilot sessions from one menu bar icon or macOS desktop widget. Every source is strictly opt-in—you only enable what you actually use. On-Device Apple Intelligence Summaries: Instead of dumping raw notification lists, brief-bar uses Apple's on-device Foundation Models to generate a quick brief of what needs your attention. Because it runs 100% locally via Apple Intelligence, there are no extra API keys to configure and your work metadata never leaves your Mac. Zero Electron Bloat: Built natively with SwiftUI and WidgetKit so it uses minimal memory and feels like a built-in part of macOS. You can install it directly via Homebrew or compile it from source: brew tap mnsn/brief-bar

items.summary: The privacy issues over the company’s surveillance cameras have caused protests in schools all over the country Angela Nguyen, a senior at Stanford University, has been on a mission to make sure her school doesn’t use automated license plate readers, like those made by Flock Safety, for mass surveillance. The 21-year-old computer science major helped collect hundreds of signatures earlier this year from students, faculty, alumni and residents to demand that Stanford drop its current Flock contract and codify safeguards for similar tech tools the school may use in the future. The fear, Nguyen says, is that these cameras, which show where a vehicle was at a certain point in time, can be exploited to victimize vulnerable people. Stanford cut ties with Flock this summer, and it’s not alone. The privacy reckoning over the company’s surveillance cameras is gaining momentum at schools nationwide. Since April, at least ten university campuses across seven states, have scrapped contracts with Flock. items.title: Eliminating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference with Integer-Only Arithmetic (15 minute read)
items.summary: A floating-point number stores a fixed number of significant digits and a separate exponent. When two numbers with very different exponents are added, the small one has to be shifted to line up with the big one, and the digits that fall off on the end are gone. That means that (a+b)+c is not always equal to a+(b+c). This post looks at what happens when integer addition, which is exact, is used.

items.title: LLMs can learn some multi-step reasoning on filler tokens instead of visible CoT (9 minute read)

They also mapped theoretical layer-depth limits and showed empirical walls, with some tasks learned out to 60 steps and others failing after one to three. The work is meant to separate filler-token reasoning from steganographic hidden reasoning when interpreting chain-of-thought.

items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.
